MR. BRASSARD (CHICOUTIMI)-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "LA PRESSE"
speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) raised a point of privilege regarding a letter published in La Presse of Montreal for April 9, 1960. I could attempt to seek refuge in the fact that his intervention came rather late, but I want to say I had never intended to question the impartiality of the deputy chairman of the house, or that of his assistant.
The sole burden of my complaint in the letter in question was that it is sometimes difficult for a new member, who is not in the habit of rising very often and does not know too much about parliamentary usage to catch the eye of the person chairing the committees.
Let me add that, if what I wrote could be construed as even an implicit reflection on the deputy speaker or his assistant, I consider it a pleasure and a duty to withdraw what may have been interpreted as a charge or even an insinuation of partiality.
I appreciate that the task of the person presiding over a committee of the whole house is not at all an easy one, and if, unintentionally, I have caused him any pain or embarrassment, I sincerely regret it, and I hope that both he and the house will accept my most sincere apologies.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. BRASSARD (CHICOUTIMI)-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "LA PRESSE"
speechtext:
The hon. member for Chicoutimi has made a statement which the house has heard. The matter was raised yesterday, as hon. members will recall, as a question of privilege and a motion was tendered which was reserved until the hon. member was in his place. The statement he has made which, if I may express an opinion, seems to be a complete retraction of anything that was offensive and a disclaimer of an intent to be offensive to the Chairman or Deputy Chairman of course will be considered by the house, by the mover of the motion and by
those who were affected, and I hope will be considered as satisfactory.
For myself, there was a reference in the extract which was read yesterday relating to the practice of recognizing hon. members in the course of debate which was somewhat erroneous. The practice has been clear, I think, throughout the years that in debate hon. members are recognized alternatively from each side of the house.
The other point raised was about a list of speakers. It is true that lists are submitted to the Chair to advise him of those who have the intention of speaking but of course the list has no binding force as has often been stated by Speakers.
Having said that I leave it up to the hon. members concerned and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, whose motion stands for disposition.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MR. BRASSARD (CHICOUTIMI)-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "LA PRESSE"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, though the hon. member for Chicoutimi referred to both the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman I, of course, can only speak for myself. However, after hearing his remarks I will be very happy to accept his apology.

subtopic: MR. BRASSARD (CHICOUTIMI)-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "LA PRESSE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not think any apology is owing to me arising out of the remarks by the hon. member for Chicoutimi, and I am not looking for that. I do think, however, that implicit in his speech was a reflection not only on the deputy chairman but also upon my position as a member of this group and of the house. I think it is worth while pointing out that in that debate from the resolution stage right through, this group had four speakers. I checked the possible time by the length of the speeches, and I think it would come to less than one-twentieth of the debate. The effect of this letter would indicate, of course, that we had taken an inordinate amount of time as some matter of right recognized by you. I believe it should be made clear that on this occasion and on all others our group has no inordinate privilege and does not claim any.
I merely wanted to say I have always had the greatest respect for the deputy chairman, but I can underline the fact that we have had no personal contact of any kind for many months, which would indicate that he was not in any secret agreement with my view.

subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON TERMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should say a word at this time regarding the abrupt termination of the summit meeting in Paris. There was an opportunity for progress and improvement at this meeting which had awakened the hopes of millions of people throughout the world. For reasons of his own, reasons which I think all members of this house regard as totally unjustifiable, Chairman Khrushchev has refused to meet with the other participants. By so doing he ended, before the sessions had properly begun, all hopes of achievement at this conference.
Any cause for complaint which the Soviet leader may have felt had been removed by President Eisenhower's assurances on May 16 that over-flights had been stopped and would not be resumed. The president did this even though there was no indication that


the Soviet union was willing to give equal assurances that objectionable activities for which it was responsible would also end.
There have been periods in the past when east-west relations were characterized by sustained acrimony, but recently it had been the expectation of people everywhere in the world that we were moving into a better era where we would solve our problems by reasonable negotiation. I think I express the views of all hon. members of tips house when I say that despite the tragic international drama of yesterday and the developments of the last few days, mankind has not been thrown all the way back into the frightening gloom of the cold war.
The NATO council will meet tomorrow. The NATO powers have been working and will continue to work toward the establishment of good relations between east and west as a basis for negotiation and settlement. It remains essential that despite the admitted setbacks of the last few days, efforts to make progress toward peace and security must not be abandoned, for the return to cold war will be as detrimental to east and west, as a relaxation of tensions will be beneficial to both.
There are only two ways in which our differences can be settled. We in the west believe in negotiation. With the collapse of the summit meeting I believe it more imperative than ever that negotiations be continued in Geneva on disarmament and on the suspension of nuclear weapons tests.
These events of the last 48 hours have confirmed the need for the western nations to remain on guard. We are now entering a period of reassessment and re-examination. The roseate hopes of the last few months have certainly been clouded in the last few hours. This is a time, however, for review and reflection, not for provocation or incitement. We should shortly learn the attitude that the Russians will adopt on disarmament, on the nuclear test talks, on Berlin and on the expansion of trade and cultural contacts. When we learn this we will know whether or not future relations will be determined in the same abrupt manner that was displayed by Chairman Khrushchev in Paris.
The restraint and dignity and high sense of purpose with which the western leaders attempted to overcome the difficulties which Mr. Khrushchev had put in the way deserve recognition and support. I want to associate the Canadian government with the views of the three western leaders as expressed in the communique just issued. The words they used were these:
They regret that these discussions, so important for world peace, could not take place. For their part they remain unshaken in their conviction that

all outstanding international questions should be settled not by the use or threat of force but by peaceful means through negotiation. They themselves remain ready to take part in such negotiations at any suitable time in the future.
Speaking again for the Canadian government I wish to say that we are ready to do anything we can appropriately do to further this policy as enunciated by the western leaders.
Finally, however deplorable Mr. Khrushchev's action in Paris, he is mistaken if he thinks he can divide the west by such tactics. On the contrary, his tactics have already served to strengthen the resolve of the western countries to remain united.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON TERMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Prime Minister's statement gives a very realistic view of the situation that confronts the world at this time. On behalf of the official opposition I should like to assure him of our wholehearted support for anything that can be done by our government in the furtherance of this viewpoint. I am sure there is no difference of opinion in the house on that.
There is no point in trying to disguise the fact that the news from Paris has been bad and perhaps is now worse in the light of the nature and content of the press conference given this morning by the leader of the Soviet union. However, this is no time for panic, any more than it is a time for yielding to the temptation to give up in the search for peace. It is also no time to weaken the unity of all peace-loving nations in that search, as the Prime Minister has so well pointed out.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that it was important to make every effort to save the conference in Paris, and also to make it quite clear where the responsibility for the failure of that conference lies. I believe the western leaders have done that. But it is equally important, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, for the west to make sure, in so far as the western countries can make sure, that the break-up of the conference does not mean the break-down of this effort to solve international problems and secure the peace.
Perhaps we of the western countries can draw some necessary conclusions from the failure of this conference. One must be as to the dangers and the disabilities of diplomacy at the summit in the circumstances in which we find ourselves today, and the desirability of conducting diplomatic negotiations, whenever and wherever possible, under the auspices of the United Nations. So it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, at this time more than

The Prime Minister has mentioned a meeting of the NATO council, I think he said tomorrow, and I think that is a good development. Perhaps the government has already given consideration to the desirability of a minister being in Paris, if that is possible, in view of the fact that the foreign ministers of three western countries presumably will be attending that meeting.
In any event, whatever the government does on this, they can be assured of the wholehearted support of the opposition in any move they may make to ease the situation and strengthen our chances for peace.

subtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON TERMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. group were impressed by the restraint, constructive tone and content of the Prime Minister's statement. We agree with the general tenor of his remarks, and he can be assured, as Prime Minister of this country, that he will have the full support of the C.C.F. party in any efforts made by Canada in the important work toward peace that lies ahead.
It was exceedingly regrettable to see the summit conference disintegrate. We have expressed, on previous occasions, our criticism of the U-2 spy plane incident. We feel that was a mistake. But even with that mistake having been made, this was no excuse for Premier Khrushchev to torpedo the peaceful hopes of tens of millions of people in the world. We are impressed by and appreciative of the continuing good work which has been done by Prime Minister Macmillan in attempting to bring the heads of governments together, and by his attempt to salvage something before the conference disintegrated.
I noticed the Prime Minister's statement that the NATO powers will be meeting tomorrow to discuss this situation. I would hope the NATO powers would resist any temptation to mimic the bluster and threat of the Soviet leader. This is no time, in our opinion, for the rattling of swords or for the taking of a threatening posture. This is the time for the NATO powers to show unity, yes, and a fervent desire for peace and an amicable settlement. We hope the Geneva conference discussions will continue, and that from this conference may be salvaged some type of agreement.
No matter what the antics of the various leaders of the world, we are convinced that the peoples of the world want peace, whether those peoples live in the Soviet union, in the United States or in any other nation of

Communications
the world. And mankind will judge the leaders of all nations on the basis of their integrity, their sincerity and their willingness to compromise in the interests of peace. We hope that even with these disastrous climaxes to the summit conference steps will be taken in the near future to improve trade relations, to go forward with cultural exchanges and to continue-yes, if possible on an increasing scale-the interchange of visits between peoples of all the nations of the world.
At this time we are hopeful that the United Nations may be able to take action that will strengthen the cause of peace, whether this action be through a meeting of the United Nations security council or a meeting of the general assembly. No matter with which party one sits in the Canadian House of Commons, I think all of us are determined to do our best as we see it in the interests of peace, coexistence, mutual understanding and the preservation of the ideals that we hold so dear.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I reiterate that the Canadian government in every effort it puts forward, whether it be by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)., the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) or any other representative, will have the complete and wholehearted support of the C.C.F. while we are convinced that these efforts are being directed toward the firmer establishment of peace in the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF EMERGENCY CONTROL ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has had under consideration for some time the problem of arranging for effectual governmental control of the national telecommunications systems under nuclear war conditions. The conclusion has now been reached that if the government as a whole, its various agencies and private users with essential wartime functions, are to make the best use of the telecommunications services available after a nuclear attack, it is necessary to develop an emergency organization which would exist in nucleus form in peacetime as a planning agency, and in emergency would function as the executive agency of government in controlling and administering the national communications systems including radio and television broadcasting.
The organization is to be known as the emergency national telecommunications organization, or ENTO. It will be developed within the Department of Transport and be under the control of the Minister of Transport in whom, by virtue of the Radio Act,

the Telegraph Act, the Railway Act and the Canada Shipping Act, extensive authority over telecommunications in Canada is already vested.
In the discharge of its responsibility ENTO will be advised by a committee of senior representatives of other government departments having a major interest in telecommunications. Advice from commercial telecommunication agencies will also be sought.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) for the second reading of Bill No. S-5, to incorporate the Oshawa harbour commissioners.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR MANAGEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF HARBOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were entertained last night with some criticisms of the minister who is bringing in this bill from the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), the gist of which was that the minister and the government had failed properly to present surveys which would work out some kind of schedule for the expansion of ports such as Oshawa in relation to some master plan. We welcome this urge to socialistic planning which has
Oshawa Harbour Commissioners been pushed by the hon. member for Laurier, and on behalf of this group I must express our disappointment at the introductory statement made by the minister.
I thought that if the minister could not, at least the hon. member from Oshawa, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), could have given us a little more general information about the matter. It is very difficult to know what is involved when you come from another part of the country or from a community similar to Oshawa but not in a metropolitan area. If you look at the map you will see that the harbour at Oshawa is a mile and a half from two railway tracks and several miles from the centre of town. It is not a developed harbour according to any impression one gets. There does not seem to be much at the harbour at the present time, although of course this has nothing to do with the capacity for growth.
To develop harbours costs a tremendous amount of money today, as we all know. One wonders why Oshawa wishes to have this commission if it is merely to administer the rather small properties which presently exist in the harbour. Surely in the community there is some master plan or vision of what they want to achieve. We have had no explanation with regard to that, which I would have thought would have been proper at this stage of the bill. It is apparent that Toronto has had tremendous harbour developments. Is it going to need a series of satellite harbours in the area to handle, for example, terminal traffic which would be distributed by buses? Is it the desire or hope that Oshawa harbour should eventually ship products overseas from its wharves? What is involved in terms of expanding Oshawa harbour to serve ocean-going ships which might take the products of the automobile factories abroad?
It seems to me that information like this should be given and put on the record. As it is, one is led to believe from the very brief statement of the minister that there might be a great deal of substance in the charges made by the hon. member for Laurier. I come from an area where the federal government has pumped millions of dollars over a very long time into a harbour and can appreciate what a drain on resources it is. There are a whole host of harbours along the St. Lawrence seaway and up into the great lakes which have had dreams or hopes of development on the seaway. The hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell) is not in the house, but I know from talking to him that Cornwall had such dreams. I know that Port Credit has thought a great deal about its future, as well as other ports up along

Oshawa Harbour Commissioners Georgian bay and lake Huron which have looked forward very much to such development.
Is this a case where Oshawa has been attracted by the bubble of the seaway, or is it just a very hard little group which has not any great prospect of drawing on large federal funds or even on provincial funds to develop a big harbour which fits into some sort of plan for servicing the metropolitan area of Toronto? I think we deserve this information and should be given it before second reading is over. I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), as he has told us, is so busy in other places that he cannot keep a hand on the myriad of detail in his department, but perhaps we could expect some information from the hon. member for Ontario. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that before consent is given to second reading the hon. minister from Oshawa will be kind enough to enlighten us on the future prospects of this harbour, something which perhaps the Minister of Transport out of courtesy has left for him rather than invade his field as spokesman for the city of Oshawa.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR MANAGEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF HARBOUR
speechtext:
I am only going by the reputation which has been established in this respect by the great city of Oshawa. It has a population within its own boundaries of over 58,000 people. I do not know how big Port Arthur is as far as population is concerned, but I do not imagine it is much bigger than Oshawa. Industry has gradually saturated the areas west of Toronto and


people are looking forward to locating themselves immediately east of the city of Toronto along the double lane highway, highway 401, the railway tracks and the harbour facilities which are available in this locality.
We have had a harbour for many years. It is not a large harbour compared with the ones at Port Arthur or Windsor, but it has been a very good harbour and a very useful one for the transportation of many materials which are produced nearby and for bringing in materials necessary for the livelihood of our community and the surrounding area. The industrial commissioners of the city of Oshawa have laid aside many acres of land running immediately north of the harbour for industrial development. They are planning on putting this forward. At the moment I am advised that a number of industries from outside Canada are particularly interested in locating here providing they have proper harbour facilities. This necessitates additional wharves because this area is on the opposite side of the present harbour facilities. We have had a team of people representing the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport come and assess the situation. Their reports are very favourable for the future. The location is excellent and as I say industry is inquiring about locating providing we can make these additional facilities available to them.
In order to have good, planned harbour facilities, city of Oshawa officials, the council and others interested, such as the industrial committee and the chamber of commerce, have asked that a commission be established so that they can devote their time to the orderly planning of their harbour for the future. I think it is a very wise and good housekeeping move to do this so that these things can be planned in order to bring about the maximum of good facilities which may be required in the future.

I should like to take this opportunity to make a few brief observations on this measure, not only with regard to Windsor but to all harbours and commissions.
As I understand it, there are three categories of harbours-those under the national harbour commissions themselves-and this includes, I believe, some 2,300 such harbours; those such as is now being proposed in Oshawa, and that in Windsor, and the ports in Hamilton, Toronto and New Westminster. If what the hon. gentleman has just said is true, and I do not believe it is, that what the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) was arguing, and what I was saying on the Windsor bill only points out that the previous administration should have taken this very


step. I do not agree with that but assume for argument's sake that that is the case. Let us address ourselves to the particular situation. Hon. members opposite do not always need to say, "Well, the previous government did not do this or that." That may or may not be the situation. The point is, what can we do right now? The St. Lawrence seaway has been built. It is now a fact. It was formally opened while the present minister was in office. We want to take the fullest advantage of this great achievement in which the Canadian people have great pride and in order to do that, as I said last night, we ought to give to all of the ports on the great lakes equal opportunity for sharing in the achievement of the St. Lawrence seaway.
The port in Toronto, I notice, had an increase of 28 per cent in shipping last year and the port in Montreal enjoyed a 20 per cent increase. Halifax had a record year. These are achievements of which I am sure every Canadian will be proud and particularly the cities involved but what we want to see is other ports in other areas given an equal opportunity.
I can see great possibilities if the federal government will come to the assistance of local boards, giving some financial and other kinds of assistance such as some of the knowhow which only the federal department has. There are some limitations in the know-how of some local communities in this work and there are certainly limited funds.
My own city of Windsor is a good example. We have lots of unemployment there. I am sure that if an imaginative approach is taken to this problem what now seems to be a limited opportunity can expand into a great opportunity for that community and in consequence for the country. As was pointed out, the Detroit river presents more river traffic than any other area in the world and if we will apply an imaginative approach to this problem we can see to it that the harbour in Windsor and that in Oshawa become great harbours, just as the harbours in Toronto, Hamilton and New Westminster have become great harbours. This will not happen unless a progressive policy is pursued by everyone in getting business.
In the case of Toronto they have the money now because of their great expansion and were able to send a Mr. Louis W. Byrne to New York where he has established an office for the purpose of drumming up business. I admire this aggressiveness on the part of the Toronto harbour commission and I would like to see the same thing done for my own

city as I am sure the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) would like to see done for his. It cannot be expected that the mere setting up of a harbour commission in these places can accomplish that without having some help particularly in the beginning.
Financial help has been given to New Westminster and Hamilton as the minister knows. I am sure if the minister will address himself to the great vision of making sure that the achievement of the St. Lawrence seaway is made a reality to all communities where opportunities can be taken in that particular context, the vision I have portrayed will be found to be not an impossible one. I would hope that when the minister replies he would give some indication of his intentions in this regard.
I know that all governments, and properly so, want to be careful about incurring unnecessary expenditure. They want to give as much reliance to local effort as possible. That is commendable but that is not to say there are not situations where assistance from the federal authority to the community is not justified. In this instance I believe there is a strong argument for assistance. This was the view of the committee of 1958 when they made the unanimous recommendation referred to last evening and found at page 150 of the proceedings of that committee:
The committee recommends for the consideration of the department the establishment of an economic survey to consider the effects of the St. Lawrence seaway project upon all regions of Canada.
I am not talking now about surveys of individual ports. This recommendation goes away beyond that. It calls for a survey to consider the effects of the St. Lawrence seaway project upon all regions. The fact is that has not been done. I do not think it is too strong to say that at the present time there has been no change whatever in the approach taken by the government to the various ports. There has been no thinking, no policy, no action. Nothing at all has been done. I am surprised because the minister who is not by any means without his imperfections is nevertheless a vigorous minister who addresses himself courageously to all matters that come within the compass of his activities. I would hope that the vigour and imagination which we know him to possess would be utilized in meeting this objective and in doing so it would further the purposes of the ports in Oshawa and Windsor-the latter of which interests the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer) and myself in a special way-and other harbours.
I think there is a broad national interest in this problem. It is one that cannot be

When he was speaking yesterday, the hon. member for Laurier left the impression with the house that he felt that harbour commissions should not be set up until a full-scale economic study had been made of the whole St. Lawrence seaway and its effect on all parts of Canada. I shall quote what he said in that regard, as reported at page 3989 of Hansard, righthand column:
-an economic survey should be made by the officers oi the Department of Transport with reference to the impact which the St. Lawrence seaway would have upon the various regions of Canada.
We should not go ahead, he claimed, with these harbour commissions until such a survey had been made. The government has been very much aware of the desirability of proper economic planning with regard to the development and use of ports in the St. Lawrence and great lakes area, particularly in view of the changes resulting from the construction of the seaway. However, a purely theoretical study, as suggested by the hon. member for Laurier, carried out by planners having little contact with the realities of local situations and having a cosmic or over-all approach which would be so general as to offer no guide to the solution of local problems, did not appear to us to be a reasonable solution to this matter even though it is obviously the sort of thing which the hon. member for Laurier had in mind.
Rather, Mr. Speaker, we felt that the best answer lay in close contact with local organizations and officials in the towns and cities bordering the seaway and great lakes in regard to their local port problems, and a continuing series of visits as and when requested by local officials for this purpose. With this in mind we organized in 1957, after forming the government, a special team composed of marine representatives, technical, engineering and construction personnel and economic staff from the Department of Transport and Department of Public Works for the purpose of visiting those ports and making special studies and reports in each case. This team consisted of the director of marine works, or his representative, from the Department of Transport; the senior economist from the bureau of economic studies of the Department of Transport; the director of economic studies, or his representative, of the Department of Public Works; and the chief of harbours and rivers construction division, or his representative, of the Department of Public Works.
Whenever a request is received from a port town or city we make prompt arrangements

for a visit by this team and in the course of this visit they make not only a study of port conditions and requirements but they also meet with municipal officials, chamber of commerce representatives and the representatives of large local businesses interested in shipping in order to get the most complete and effective advice and information available.
Following this, the team makes a special report on the situation to myself and to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and jointly we proceed with our planning in the light of the information contained in the reports. Moreover, because of the great number of places visited by this group, they, together with the officials of my department to whom they report, are in an excellent position to take a sound, over-all view of the whole problem of the great lakes and the St. Lawrence in the light of the comprehensive data which they have gathered on individual points.
I would point out particularly that this visiting team was not organized until October, 1957; that is, it was not organized under the previous government but was organized a few short months after we rescued this country from the late lamented Liberal government in 1957. But in the period since it was organized its work has involved special trips to and reports on the following ports, and I intend to give them because I think they are interesting, Mr. Speaker. What is it that makes a harbour a potential harbour for the future? In so far as incoming shipments are concerned, this potential depends on two things: first of all, whether the municipality is a market for manufactured goods or is suitable as a distribution centre to other markets; second, whether the municipality has industries which require bulk cargoes, and whether there are suitable transportation facilities to industries in the vicinity. In so far as outgoing shipments are concerned, the potential depends on whether the municipality or surrounding localities have two things, I believe: first of all, industries which produce manufactured goods for shipment to other parts of Canada or to other countries; and, second, industries which produce bulk cargoes for shipment to other parts of Canada or to other countries.
The businessmen of our ports know these factors very well indeed. Those who are appointed by us to be harbour commissioners are particularly well versed in these facts. Mr. Speaker, a petition sponsored jointly by the corporation of the city of Nanaimo and the Nanaimo chamber of commerce was received in my department regarding a proposal to establish a harbour commission for the harbour of Nanaimo, British Columbia. The city would upon the enactment of the necessary legislation vest in the proposed harbour commission harbour front property owned by the city for management and development by the commissioners.
It is considered advisable in the interests of proper and orderly development and expansion of the Nanaimo harbour that control be vested in a local body. The harbour is a natural, all year round deep sea harbour and is protected from the open waters of the straits of Georgia by the outer island of Gabriola and by the inner islands of Newcastle and Protection.
The strategic location of the harbour provides a loading and unloading point for the two main ferry services connecting Vancouver island and the lower mainland, that is Canadian Pacific railway and Black Ball Ferries Limited. During the peak of the summer season the ferries carry upwards of 1,250,000 passengers, 300,000 passenger cars and 50,000 trucks and trailers.
My department operates the government assembly wharf and the deep sea wharf which are approximately 1150 feet in length. They are used for the handling of lumber, pulpwood, fuel oil, iron ore, chemicals and other products from which a gross annual income is derived of approximately $30,000. These facilities would be placed under the management of the commisioners. In addition, the department collects in the neighbourhood of $16,000 annually in harbour dues and some $23,000 annually in water lot leases. This revenue would also be immediately available to the harbour commissioners.
The purpose of the bill is to establish a harbour commission to administer the harbour. There will be three commissioners, two appointed by the governor in council and

one by the city of Nanaimo. It is a bill similar to the one which set up the lakehead and other harbour commissions.
As already indicated, I propose to move after second reading that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Newfoundland Fisheries I notice that by this bill-and this is true of other bills establishing harbour commissions in other places-the commission is given borrowing powers; it is given authority to issue debentures and borrow money for the purposes required. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this bill will be brief, merely by way of explanation and to establish the authority for the action which is now proposed.
At present, under term 22 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada, certain fisheries laws, as defined in paragraph (1) of term 22, in so far as they relate to the export marketing of salted fish from Newfoundland to other countries or to any province of Canada, have been continued in force in the province of Newfoundland for a period of five years from the date of union and thereafter until the parliament of Canada otherwise provides.
Under term 18 of the said terms of union all laws in force in Newfoundland at, or immediately prior to the date of union, have been continued therein as if the union had not been made, subject to repeal or alteration by the parliament of Canada or the legislature of the province of Newfoundland according to the authority of the parliament or the legislature under the British North America Acts 1867 to 1946. Likewise, all orders, rules and regulations made under any such laws have been continued subject to revocation or amendment by the appropriate constitutional authority.
In 1959, the exportation of salt fish (permits) act, being No. 10 of the statutes of Newfoundland, 1942, and being one of the

statutes listed in paragraph (1) of term 22, was repealed by the parliament of Canada.
The remaining statutes listed in paragraph (1) of term 22 relate to the Newfoundland fisheries board, which board, under and by virtue of paragraphs (2) and (5) of term 22. have been brought within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. The board has been continued to date.
Since the proclamation in Newfoundland of the fisheries act on May 1, 1958, the proclamation in Newfoundland of the meat and canned foods act and the fish inspection act on July 1, 1959, and the repeal of the exportation of salt fish (permits) act as of August 1, 1959, the board has ceased to have any functions.
The purpose of the proposed legislation is to repeal, pursuant to terms 18 and 22, the remaining statutes which are listed in paragraph (1) of term 22 and which have been consolidated by the province of Newfoundland in the Newfoundland fisheries board act, being chapter 207 of the revised statutes of Newfoundland, 1952, and to repeal all orders, rules and regulations made thereunder, or made pursuant thereto under the terms of union.
In short, the Newfoundland fisheries laws, as defined under term 22 of the terms of union with Canada, are now redundant and serve no useful purpose. These laws have been superseded by the statutes of Canada relating to fisheries which have now been brought into force in Newfoundland.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on the act which we are about to repeal. This act had its roots in attempts made to standardize control of the marketing of dried salted codfish in particular. In the days prior to confederation and in the years immediately following, inspection or, to use the time-honoured word, "culling" had to do with grading of fish, and not only grading of fish for export but those regulations were two-pronged. Government inspection began when fishermen were selling their fish. Cullers would sort out the fish as it was being delivered to the merchant by the fishermen. The culler would separate the fish into various grades and the fishermen would be paid accordingly. The final act of inspection would be when the fish was ready for export. It would be inspected to make sure that the quality was as marked in order to maintain the standards of the fish in our markets.
The effect of this repeal bill will be that federal inspection will be limited to inspection for export. Personally I do not see too much wrong with this move. Quality as between merchant and fisherman is not really the business of the federal government. My own opinion is that when fish is in good 79951-0-254!
Newfoundland Fisheries demand the cull is easy. Competitors will pay high prices for a lower grade article rather than stick to strict grading and pay overly high prices. This redounds to the benefit of the fisherman. When the market is slow the culling regulations can be used as a stick to beat down prices and this redounds against the interests of the fisherman. Unless there were a strict policy of anchoring prices to grades I cannot see that federal or other control of fish as between the fisherman and the merchant can be of real benefit to the fisherman.
I think I should say, however, that easy culling and the lack of premium prices for premium grades do not encourage quality production. I intend to say more about this later on the fisheries estimates. However, the ancient practice of easy or hard culling, depending on market conditions will not pass away overnight. I doubt whether any legislation can eradicate it. Only time, industrialization or the extinction of the codfish will end it.
But there is much to be said for paying a premium on quality and unless there is a better price for a quality article the incentive to produce really good fish is somewhat limited. Fortunately most fishermen take pride in their work and do the very best they can. Such men should get a reward by way of a better price for the better article produced. The ideal situation would be a fair set of culling regulations which would be adhered to and a price set in accordance with quality.
Before union the Newfoundland fisheries laws were administered by the Newfoundland fisheries board. The board's authority covered the grading or culling of fish. Fish were culled when they changed hands from fishermen to merchants. The fish were inspected and graded before being shipped to the markets. I think I should say that quality has much to do with whether or not we retain our markets. I am convinced that every incentive should be offered and every care should be taken to see that Canadian fish is good fish. It is interesting to note that the world consumption of fish is increasing but that our production compared with the world increase in consumption is not keeping pace.
Much of the world's fish is caught off the east coast of Canada by foreign ships. I have gone into this matter before and shall not do so now. I feel, however, that I must emphasize again the need for recognition that in our fisheries we have a source of really great potential wealth. Yet only about 10 per cent of the world consumption of salted fish, which is estimated at half a million tons per year, is produced in Canada, which should be the greatest producer of fish in the world.
Quality must be maintained and markets developed. Culling regulations and inspection

Newfoundland Fisheries generally have a direct bearing on the article for sale. The final effect is what counts. The amount of fish we sell, the condition it is in when it reaches the markets and the way marketing is conducted are prime factors in the industry. I should like to include in my remarks an appeal for an aggressive marketing policy. I should like to emphasize that much has been done in recent years to assist the fisherman but much has yet to be done to round out a complete program. Finally, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) to give his personal attention to the matter of aggressive marketing of Canadian fish.

Mr. Speaker, it has been very interesting to listen to the lucid explanation of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Granger) with respect to the Newfoundland fishing industry and the effect that the passage of the bill before us will have. He also referred to other matters about which he is concerned. We in the C.C.F. wish to indicate to the house and to the people of Newfoundland who will be affected by the bill that we support the bill.
If I may be allowed to venture into this field to a slight extent, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador related some of the difficulties experienced between the fishermen and the buyers with respect to the price paid for fish and the grading of fish. If I may be allowed to say so, I suggest that this difficulty can be overcome to a degree by the development of co-operative ownership of the various sections of the fishing industry so that the fishermen themselves can have far greater control over grading and prices and can establish a degree of uniformity with respect to prices and grades that will greatly enhance their economic position.
In those places where co-operatives are not possible or have not been formed, I suggest that the development of some form of union would be helpful in protecting the interests of the fishermen. I think it can be said that generally fishermen on the west coast and others connected with the industry have had a very good experience with the federal Department of Fisheries not only with respect to the inspection services but in the field of conservation and all the other fields in which the federal department is involved. I hope sincerely that the people of Newfoundland who will be affected by the passage of this bill will have the same beneficial experience with the Department of Fisheries that we on the west coast have had.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the chair.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Before clause 1 carries, if the minister will permit me I should like to echo the appeal of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador with respect to the need for the most aggressive possible marketing policy. As the minister has told us, under the legislation now being repealed there were provisions for marketing through a marketing board and through other agencies that will no longer be open under the laws of Canada which will supersede the legislation now being repealed.
As my hon. friend said in his speech, we have no quarrel with that position. But we are very gravely concerned, as I am sure the government, the minister, the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister without Portfolio are with a proposal that has been made by the common market, which happily has now been adjourned for some little time, to put a tariff around the whole common market area in Europe against Canadian codfish. The effect of that, if it were to be carried out, would of course be to give the French producers, who have a base eight miles off the coast of Newfoundland a differential advantage in a market where they have never had it before and would, to that extent, be a disability which would have to be overcome either by price cutting or by some other device which would be bound, in the end, to bring a lower return to our fishermen. We might, indeed, lose the market altogether.
Unhappily in the last few years, although the market has not been too bad itself, the production of the kind of fish that is required by the Italian market and also by the Spanish market has been going down and the production of the kind of fish that can be sold only in the West Indies has been going up. The consequence of this is that we are losing sales in a good market and tending, to some degree, to congest the supply in another market, to the disadvantage of all Canadian producers. I just echo very strongly the words of my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, that the government should give very careful consideration to the possibility of doing what was done before the war in order to supply the British market with bacon, that is to say, the establishment of a premium-perhaps for a year or two to see how it would work-on the Spanish and Italian fish in order to try to keep that market during the technological revolution of which I am sure the minister is aware on the east coast. What is going on at Valleyfield

and elsewhere offers a real hope that it will not be very long before light salted fish can be produced in plants. Then it may be possible to survive in these markets without any need for a premium and allowing purely economic forces to operate. There is very grave danger, in the interval, of losing the market.
I noticed in an item in the newspapers only last night our ambassador to Spain was talking about the failure of Canadians to take advantage of the market in Spain. I do not know whether that is true, but this is one market, in Spain, which we know is the best market of all pricewise. If we can only make sure of hanging on to it for the next two or three years I think there would be a real hope of keeping it for good. It is very important, not merely in an isolated way but as part of the over-all picture of the markets in that area.
Perhaps, sir, if you construed the bill very narrowly you might find a little difficulty in ascertaining that my remarks were actually relevant. However, in view of the fact that this is really carrying out part of the terms of union, you would not wish to do that and perhaps you would wish to give the minister an opportunity to say a word in reply.

The suggestions made by the two members from Newfoundland who have spoken on this bill are helpful and constructive. I express the hope that they will continue to draw to the attention of the committee problems that may arise with regard to the fishing industry.
From the standpoint of the Department of Trade and Commerce, working very closely in co-operation with the Department of Fisheries, we want to do everything that is within our power to maintain the Canadian export market for fish. We put forth the same effort with regard to this product as we do with other products that are exported from Canada. The export of fish from Canada, as from the earliest days, has been one of the great factors in our economy and should be maintained.
We are watching continuously the developments in Europe with regard to the establishment of a common market and free trade area. From time to time we have put forward, and will continue in the future to put forward, Canada's position with regard to that market. Our position is one of concern lest it should
